blockMcqs.question: Which metric does QoS primarily protect for real-time traffic?
blockMcqs.explanation: QoS ensures real-time flows (voice, video) get low latency and scheduling priority over bulk traffic.

blockMcqs.question: A 1 Gbps link has 20% packet loss. What best describes throughput?
options: Still 1 Gbps — loss doesn't affect throughput
Less than 1 Gbps — loss reduces useful data delivered
Greater than 1 Gbps — retransmits add capacity
blockMcqs.explanation: Throughput is the actual data delivered; packet loss forces retransmissions and reduces effective throughput below bandwidth.

blockMcqs.question: What does the `ping` command primarily measure?
blockMcqs.explanation: Ping sends an ICMP echo and reports the round-trip time — the total time for the packet to go and come back.

blockMcqs.question: Why is even 1% packet loss severe for VoIP?
options: It causes audible glitches that TCP retransmits can't hide in real time
blockMcqs.explanation: VoIP is real-time; TCP retransmits arrive too late to help. Any lost audio frame causes audible distortion.

blockMcqs.question: Which latency component is fixed by the physical distance of the path?
blockMcqs.explanation: Propagation delay depends on distance and the speed of light — it cannot be reduced without moving endpoints closer.

blockMcqs.question: A link has 100 Mbps bandwidth and 200 ms RTT. What is its bandwidth-delay product?
blockMcqs.explanation: BDP = 100 Mbps × 0.2 s = 20 Mb = 2.5 MB. TCP must have this much data in flight to saturate the link.

blockMcqs.question: What does the DSCP field in an IP header support?
blockMcqs.explanation: DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point) marks packets with a priority class so routers can apply QoS scheduling.

blockMcqs.question: What problem does bufferbloat cause?
options: Excessive latency from overly large router buffers
Higher jitter on bulk transfers only
blockMcqs.explanation: Large buffers absorb bursts but queue packets for hundreds of milliseconds, making latency-sensitive apps unusable.
